w: Built in just 38 years between 1220 and 1258, giving it an unusual unity among medieval English cathedrals. Its spire, finished by 1330 and standing 404 feet, is the tallest in England, a title it gained after Lincoln's and Old St Paul's spires collapsed. Pevsner called its close the most beautiful in England.
s: England's tallest spire, built in just 38 years
_facts: Built 1220-1258; tower and spire completed by 1330
Spire is 404 ft, the tallest in England
Cloisters added 1240, chapter house 1263
Cathedral Close is Britain's largest

w: The abandoned first Salisbury, settled since 3000 BC and fortified as an Iron Age hillfort by 400 BC. Romans, Saxons and Normans each took it in turn; Henry I built a royal palace inside its castle. Disputes finally drove the cathedral down onto the plain, and the old hilltop town was dismantled for stone.
s: The abandoned hilltop town Salisbury replaced
_facts: Iron Age hillfort from around 400 BC; settlement traces to 3000 BC
Norman motte-and-bailey castle and stone cathedral built here
Royal palace built for Henry I within the castle
Abandoned once New Salisbury and its cathedral rose on the plain

w: A Grade I listed Elizabethan prodigy house on the banks of the Avon south of Salisbury, still the seat of the Earl of Radnor. Prodigy houses were built by Elizabethan courtiers expressly to dazzle: vast, showy piles designed to impress a monarch who might one day visit.
s: An Elizabethan showpiece on the River Avon
_facts: Grade I listed country house on the River Avon
Example of the Elizabethan prodigy house
Seat of the Earl of Radnor

w: The first cathedral of the Bishops of Salisbury, standing at Old Sarum from 1092 until 1220. Only its foundations remain, traced out in the northwest quadrant of the old hillfort's outer bailey, the original source of the Sarum Rite that shaped English liturgy for centuries.
_facts: Catholic cathedral at Old Sarum, 1092-1220
Only foundations survive, in the outer bailey
Original source of the Sarum Rite

w: The last of four medieval market crosses in Salisbury, marking a market site since 1307. The 14th-century stone structure lost its flying buttresses in 1711, visible in Turner's 1800 painting, before new ones were rebuilt in the 1850s. Salisbury Market still gathers here every Tuesday and Saturday.
s: The last of Salisbury's four medieval market crosses
_facts: Market site dates to 1307; present structure 14th century
Original flying buttresses removed 1711, painted by Turner in 1800
Buttresses rebuilt 1852-1854 by architect Owen Browne Carter
Salisbury Market still held here on Tuesdays and Saturdays

w: A Grade I listed parish church with a chancel dating to around 1230, a 14th-century spired tower and a 15th-century nave. Restored in 1849-50 by Thomas Henry Wyatt and David Brandon, its Anglo-Catholic parish still rejects the ordination of women, receiving oversight instead from the Bishop of Oswestry.
s: A medieval parish church under Oswestry's bishop
_facts: Chancel built c.1230; tower and spire 14th century
Restored 1849-50 by Wyatt and Brandon
Grade I listed since 1952
Anglo-Catholic parish overseen by the Bishop of Oswestry

w: An 18th-century municipal building standing in the Market Place, still the meeting place of Salisbury City Council today. A Grade II* listed civic landmark, it anchors the market square that has been the heart of the city since medieval times.
_facts: 18th-century municipal building in the Market Place
Grade II* listed
Still the meeting place of Salisbury City Council

w: A Grade I listed schoolroom in Salisbury's Cathedral Close, rebuilt in 1714 by Thomas Naish to house the cathedral choristers, funded by Sir Stephen Fox in tribute to Wiltshire-born Christopher Wren. Old headmaster's and assistant's desks still sit at opposite ends of the Big School Room, with medieval cellars below.
s: A choristers' schoolroom in the Cathedral Close
_facts: Rebuilt 1714 by Thomas Naish, funded by Sir Stephen Fox
Named in tribute to Christopher Wren, though little proven link to him
Original desks remain from its use as the 'Big School Room'
Medieval cellars survive below the building

w: A ruined medieval royal residence about 2.25 miles east of Salisbury, where the Assize of Clarendon was held, developing the Constitutions of Clarendon, a landmark moment in English legal history. The ruins now sit quietly within the grounds of Clarendon Park.
s: Ruins where the Constitutions of Clarendon were born
_facts: Medieval royal residence, ruined, 2.25 miles east of Salisbury
Site of the Assize of Clarendon
Developed the Constitutions of Clarendon
Now within the grounds of Clarendon Park
